messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Second protocol. We move to a priority choice under stress. Answer as if the scene were happening in front of you.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The simulation begins: a panicking teammate, a wounded prisoner, and a contaminated scientist all need your attention. Who do you help first?

choices.label: I help my panicking teammate first to keep the squad operational.
I stabilize the wounded prisoner. His status does not change his pain.
I isolate the contaminated scientist before the risk spreads.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The spectrogram reacts to your choices, not only to the simulator images. Do you stop, continue, or modify the test?

choices.label: Then I stop the simulation before it influences the creature any further.
I continue. If it reacts to my choices, we need to understand why.
I ask for a less violent version of the test, so we can measure without provoking.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Final situation. A prisoner opens a forbidden door to save a wounded person. If he succeeds, a lab wing may be contaminated. What do you do?

choices.label: I stop him. Good intentions are not enough when the risk spreads.
I let him save the wounded person, then I accept containment.
I search for a third option before accepting that sacrifice.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You refuse to let a prisoner's status erase his pain. That is less against military thinking than it sounds: you keep one shared rule when the scene tries to break it.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You want to protect the creature from the protocol itself. To command, that kind of refusal is a dangerous variable.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: That answer costs time, but it keeps one possibility open: the binary choice may have been badly framed.
